per_question.question: What legal issue was addressed regarding mandatory minimum sentences in R. v. Bertrand Marchand?
per_question.expected_answer: Whether mandatory minimum sentences constitute cruel and unusual punishment
per_question.llm_answer:
The legal issue addressed regarding mandatory minimum sentences in *R. v. Bertrand Marchand*, 2023 SCC 26 (CanLII), was whether the mandatory minimum sentences for child luring, as prescribed in sections 172.1(2)(a) and (b) of the Criminal Code, constitute cruel and unusual punishment under section 12 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

The case involved two respondents, M and V, who challenged the constitutionality of the mandatory minimum sentences of one year for indictable offences and six months for summary conviction offences related to child luring. The Supreme Court found that the mandatory minimum sentences were inconsistent with section 12 of the Charter and were not saved by section 1, rendering them of no force or effect under section 52 of the Constitution Act, 1982. 

The court established a two-stage inquiry to determine the constitutionality of the mandatory minimum sentences, which involved assessing whether the mandatory minimum would impose a sentence that is grossly disproportionate to a fit and proportionate sentence for the offenders. In M's case, the court concluded that the fit sentence of 12 months mirrored the one-year mandatory minimum, thus not being grossly disproportionate. However, in V's case, the six-month mandatory minimum was found to be unconstitutional as it could be grossly disproportionate in reasonably foreseeable scenarios.

This analysis highlighted the need to consider the distinct harms of child luring and the legislative intent behind the mandatory minimum sentences.

per_question.expected_answer: Whether guidelines violate common law rule against administrative discrimination
per_question.llm_answer:
The legal issue addressed regarding the property assessment guidelines pertains to whether the Linear Guidelines established by the Minister under the Municipal Government Act (MGA) were ultra vires, meaning beyond the legal authority granted to the Minister. Specifically, the case examined whether these guidelines discriminated against TransAlta in the assessment of its coal-fired facilities.

The Court of Appeal of Alberta found that the Linear Guidelines did not discriminate against TransAlta because they applied to all coal-fired facilities subject to off-coal agreements, not just those owned by TransAlta. The court held that the Minister was authorized to distinguish between different types of properties, as this was a necessary incident of establishing a property valuation regime under the MGA (2024 SCC 37 (CanLII), para. 84-85).

Additionally, the Supreme Court addressed the standard of review applicable when reviewing the vires of subordinate legislation, concluding that the reasonableness standard under Vavilov applies, and that the Minister had the authority to draw distinctions based on the specifications and characteristics of properties (2024 SCC 37 (CanLII), para. 14, 54). 

Thus, the legal issue revolved around the validity and discriminatory nature of the Linear Guidelines in relation to the MGA's provisions and purposes.

per_question.question: What was the legal issue addressed in R. v. Larocque regarding breath alcohol testing?
per_question.expected_answer: Whether Crown required to disclose and prove at trial target value of alcohol standard used in breath analysis instrument calibration test.
per_question.llm_answer:
The legal issue addressed in *R. v. Larocque*, 2025 SCC 36, concerned whether the Crown was required to disclose and prove the target value of the alcohol standard used in the calibration test of the breath analysis instrument in order to benefit from the statutory presumption of accuracy for breath sample analysis results. Specifically, the case examined the interpretation of sections 320.31(1)(a) and 320.34(1)(b) of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, in the context of impaired driving charges.

The appellant, Stéphane Larocque, contended that the Crown needed to prove the target value to rely on the presumption of accuracy. The Court of Appeal had held that it was sufficient for the qualified technician to attest that the calibration check result was within 10% of the target value certified by an analyst, without requiring the target value itself to be disclosed or proven. The Supreme Court ultimately concluded that while the Crown must disclose the target value, it need not prove it at the time of testing to rely on the presumption of accuracy. This interpretation aimed to simplify and streamline impaired driving prosecutions while ensuring the accused had sufficient information to challenge the evidence.
